tip: 'On va au supermarché': 'on' is spoken French for 'we', but the verb stays in the he/she form – 'on va', never 'on allons'.
French is 'at the phone', not on it: 'il est au téléphone', where 'au' is 'à' + 'le'. The radio works the same way – 'à la radio'.
'Chercher' already means 'look for' – the 'for' is inside it: 'cherche la gare', never 'chercher pour'. 'Attendre' (wait for) is the same.
In French, 'dans' is used for enclosed spaces: 'dans un bureau' (in an office). Use 'à' for cities and usually 'en' for countries.
In French, 'elles' is used for an all-female group. Even one male in the group changes it to 'ils'.
'Réfléchir' needs 'à' for whatever you think about: 'réfléchis à la question' = think about the question.
English lets you drop 'that' – 'he says he's busy'. French never can: 'il dit qu'il est occupé'. 'Que' shortens to 'qu'' before a vowel.
'On' has a second life as impersonal 'one/they': 'On fait les courses' can mean we do the shopping, or people in general do. Context decides.
'L'' replaces 'le' or 'la' before words starting with a vowel or silent 'h': 'l'hôtel', 'l'école', 'l'ami'.
'Du' ('de' + 'le') means 'some' before masculine nouns you can't count: 'du café', 'du lait', 'du pain'.
'Détester' = to hate. With abstract nouns, French requires the article: 'il déteste le bruit' (he hates noise).
'Excusez-moi' is formal; 'excuse-moi' is informal. The hyphen links the verb to 'moi' in commands.
For '-er' verbs ending in '-cer' ('commencer'), the 'c' becomes 'ç' before '-ons': 'nous commençons'. This keeps the soft 'c' sound.
'Est-ce que' literally means 'is it that' – put it in front of a statement and it becomes a yes/no question with no word-order change: 'Est-ce que tu connais...'.
'Un salon' is a living room, not a hair salon: 'le dîner est servi dans le salon' means dinner's served in the lounge.
Nationality adjectives agree in gender: 'français'/'française', 'anglais'/'anglaise'. They are not capitalized in French.
Adjectives with 'nous' and 'vous' forms of 'être' must agree in number: 'nous sommes fatigués' (plural '-s').
'Content' agrees in gender and number: 'content'/'contente'/'contents'/'contentes'. The final '-t' is silent in masculine forms.
'Avoir chaud' = to be hot (personal feeling). Don't confuse with 'il fait chaud' (the weather is hot).
'Avoir raison' = to be right, 'avoir tort' = to be wrong. French says 'to have reason/wrong'.
'Je suis désolé' is literally 'I am devastated' – 'désoler' means to distress. It's just the everyday way to say 'I'm sorry'.
Use 'être' for professions, with no article before the job: 'elle est médecin', not 'elle est une médecin'.
'Faire la fête' is 'to party' – literally 'to make the party'. French reaches for 'faire' where English uses 'have': 'ils font la fête'.
'Venir de' + verb means 'just did', not 'come to': 'venons de finir' = we just finished. The 'de' is what flips it to the recent past.
French can't say 'I think so' bare – it needs an object: 'je crois que oui' is literally 'I believe that yes'. The 'que oui' is fixed.
'Offrir' looks like 'offer' but usually means to give as a gift: 'elle offre des fleurs' = she gives flowers as a present, not merely offering them.
'Avoir soif' = to be thirsty. French uses 'to have thirst', not 'to be thirsty'.
'Être en retard' means to be late; 'être en avance' means to be early. Both use 'en' before the noun.
No question word, no flipped word order – just lift your voice: 'tu es malade ?' is a full question by intonation alone.
'Aller' is used for health: 'Tu vas bien ?' = Are you doing well? Literally 'You go well?'
